blocks.text: How to read
This is a fan-made field guide, laid out like the paper manuals that used to come in the box. It was written before the game came out, so it is careful about what it claims.

blocks.caption: Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, the two leads.
blocks.credit: Official Rockstar Games screenshot ("Jason and Lucia 01"), rockstargames.com/VI/media/screenshots

blocks.text: Every statement about how the game works carries a small label saying how well it is supported. Read the label before you rely on the sentence. Where the published sources disagree, the manual says so instead of picking a winner.
Nothing in this manual is official. When the game is out, each chapter will be checked against it and relabelled.
Finding

blocks.caption: Vice City at dusk.
blocks.credit: Official Rockstar Games screenshot ("Vice City 27"), rockstargames.com/VI/media/screenshots

blocks.title: Turn the page
blocks.text: Use the arrows beside the page, the left and right arrow keys, or Page Up and Page Down. On a wide window you see two pages at a time; on a narrow one, a single page.

blocks.title: Search
blocks.text: The search box at the top looks through every chapter and takes you to the page.

blocks.title: Pick up where you left off
blocks.text: The manual remembers the last page you had open. Use Continue Reading on the cover.

blocks.title: Paper or night
blocks.text: Paper View is the default. Night Reading swaps the paper for a dark page with the same layout.

blocks.title: Check the sources
blocks.text: Sources for a page are listed at its foot. The last chapter lists every source with the date it was last read.
Getting started:
What the game puts on screen, as it appears in Rockstar's own footage. The display may change before release.

blocks.caption: A shootout in an office: two bars at the top left, ammunition and the weapon at the top right.
blocks.credit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 25:16

blocks.title: Wanted stars and Heat icons
blocks.text: Top right. Up to six stars, with a row of small red icons beneath showing what the police know. The Law Enforcement chapter covers both.

blocks.title: Ammunition and weapon
blocks.text: Under the stars: two numbers and the outline of the weapon in hand. In one firefight they read 40 and 250, then 34 and 221, then 20 and 205 as the shooting goes on.
blocks.frameAlt: Four white stars, four red icons, the numbers 40 and 250, and the outline of a rifle
blocks.frameCredit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 14:12

blocks.title: Minimap
blocks.text: Bottom left: a rounded panel with buildings drawn in three dimensions, an arrow for you, a north marker on its edge, and, with a destination set, a pink route line and the distance.
blocks.frameAlt: A rounded minimap with a three-dimensional building, a pink route line and a distance of 1.86 miles
blocks.frameCredit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 8:20

blocks.title: The minimap while wanted
blocks.text: During a police chase the minimap is tinted blue in some frames and red in others.
blocks.frameAlt: A blue-tinted minimap with a small fruit-bowl icon in its top-left corner
blocks.frameCredit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 14:12

blocks.title: Heart bar and eye bar
blocks.text: Top left, seen only during a late shootout: a pink bar with a heart, and under it a purple bar with an eye. See the next page.

blocks.title: Prompts
blocks.text: Small prompts appear at the bottom right for what you can do at that moment. "Smoke" and "Throw" can be read in the footage.

items: Controls. No button layout has been published.
Whether the display can be changed or switched off.

blocks.text: Health,
Rockstar has said that eating matters and that your body changes with what you do. Several details are still unknown.

blocks.credit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 25:16 and 25:22

frames.alt: A full pink bar with a heart icon, split in two, above a full purple bar with an eye icon
frames.label: About 25:16, both full

frames.alt: The pink heart bar full and the purple eye bar about a quarter full
frames.label: About 25:22, eye bar draining

blocks.title: The bars
blocks.text: At the top left during a late shootout: a pink bar with a heart, divided into two halves by a marker, and under it a purple bar with an eye. The heart bar is full in every frame examined.
TGG, a creator who attended Rockstar's preview, reports three bars at the top left: health, stamina and Focus. The frames examined show only the two above.

blocks.title: Eating
blocks.text: Rob Nelson says eating has quite a dramatic effect on your health and gives a substantial buff.
In Famitsu's interview, read in translation, Nelson says a food buff strengthens a gauge beyond its normal maximum, and that once life falls below normal the extra is lost.

blocks.title: Where food comes from
blocks.text: In IGN's demo Jason takes a drink from the safehouse fridge. TGG reports goods being picked off a convenience store shelf and bought, an order at a drive-thru that gave a temporary boost, and a vending machine at a gym. IGN's writers saw food marked with a heart or a lightning bolt.

blocks.title: Stamina
blocks.text: In translation, Nelson says an energy drink strengthens the stamina gauge, that stamina drains with each movement of a workout, and that its base level rises with training.
TGG reports that in water the stamina bar becomes a lung-capacity meter.

blocks.title: Weight and muscle
blocks.text: Overeat and you put on weight. Gyms let you work out and go up in levels of muscularity or strength. Jason and Lucia can train together, which Nelson calls a two-for-one for managing their stats.

blocks.title: The eye bar
blocks.text: The purple bar drains from full to empty in about fourteen seconds during the office shootout, from 25:10 to 25:24. In one of those frames the whole picture is tinted red.
Nelson describes an ability called Focus, which he compares to Eagle Eye and which, as TGG relays him, can slow combat down. The eye bar is probably its meter; no source read says so outright.

blocks.title: The fruit bowl
blocks.text: A small fruit-bowl icon sits in the top-left corner of the minimap in most gameplay frames. Nothing on screen or in the sources read says what it means.

items: Whether health comes back on its own. Nelson is relayed as saying only that rest affects how some attributes regenerate.
Whether sprinting drains stamina, and what happens when it runs out.
Body armour. One creator believes it can be taken from police cars; no developer has described it.
What food exists, what it costs, and how much can be carried.
"Adrenaline": Nelson names it during a shootout and does not explain it.

blocks.text: Jason and Lucia:
You play both. How they share the game is described by Rob Nelson in IGN's interview.

blocks.title: Switching
blocks.text: You can switch between Jason and Lucia. Nelson says the team kept this as open as possible, though the story sometimes rules it out.

blocks.title: The other one carries on
blocks.text: The lead you are not playing keeps a routine: sometimes at the safehouse, sometimes out. Switch seats in a car and the other drives.

blocks.title: Safehouses
blocks.text: Nelson says safehouses are closer to the camps in Red Dead Redemption 2 than to earlier safehouses in how interactive they are. You can cut or shave your hair there; new styles need a salon or barber.

blocks.title: The relationship
blocks.text: A relationship system grows when the pair spend time together: exploring, playing pool or mini golf, kayaking, or robbing places. IGN reports that the romance is optional. Nelson says it gives no particular gameplay benefit: they stay partners in crime either way.

blocks.title: Your criminal profile
blocks.text: A separate system tracks what sort of criminal you are. Doing what a job needs is fair game; going beyond what is necessary, again and again, may shift the profile.

blocks.title: Busted
blocks.text: If either lead is arrested, it is "Busted" and a restart, as in earlier games.

items: What the criminal profile changes.
How the relationship affects the story.
Saving the game: nothing has been published.

blocks.text: The phone
Nelson says money matters more in this story than in earlier games, and that at times you must go out and earn it to move the story on.
On the phone

blocks.title: Scanner
blocks.text: Hold the phone over a vehicle to learn whether it is locked, alarmed or tracked, what it is worth at a Pay n' Spray or a specialty car fence, and what registering it for yourself would cost.

blocks.title: Snapmatic
blocks.text: You follow people and can browse it. Nelson says the pair do not post, being on the run: they just lurk.

blocks.title: Rides
blocks.text: In IGN's demo the pair travel by Ryde Me, which IGN describes as the game's version of Uber.

blocks.title: Waypoints
blocks.text: Holding down on the D-pad is a quick way to set a waypoint.
Making money

blocks.caption: Ways of earning that Nelson names or shows in the interview.
rows: Shops, banks, payday loan places; he says you can rob pretty much anything
Steal a car a fence wants and deliver it. A damaged car earns less, so it can be repaired first
A fence who will buy shows green with a dollar sign. In the demo the pair have jewelry to sell
Named among the action available in the open world

blocks.text: In translation, Nelson says cash you are carrying is at risk when you are Wasted or Busted, and is all lost if police or civilians take you down.

items: Prices, payouts and what money buys.
Property, businesses and investments.

chapters.title: Leonida & Vice City
chapters.intro: Six regions make up the State of Leonida. These are the places Rockstar has named, in its own order of billing.

chapters.title: Characters
chapters.intro: Two leads and the six supporting characters named in Rockstar's published bios.

chapters.title: Vehicles
chapters.intro: Vehicles and vehicle types seen in official material. Names appear only where Rockstar has published them.

chapters.title: Activities
chapters.intro: Things to do between missions, as shown in Rockstar's Extended Look. Footage, not a published feature list.

blocks.text: Robberies
blocks.sub: How the pair make their money

blocks.text: Rob Nelson calls robberies a huge part of what you can, and need to, do between story missions. You can rob as Jason and Lucia together or alone.

blocks.caption: Two characters tie bandanas over their faces at a door marked Open 7 Days.
blocks.credit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 11:28

blocks.text: You can rob pretty much anything.
The callout is Nelson's phrase. The targets he names are shops, banks and payday loan places, and in the demo he points at a shop that sells headphones as somewhere you could rob.
Robbery, as the footage shows it

blocks.title: Cover your face
blocks.text: At a glass door marked Open 7 Days, both characters tie bandanas over their faces before going in.

blocks.title: Go in armed
blocks.text: In a convenience store, one of them walks the aisles while the other goes to the counter and leans over it. The display shows a pistol in hand, and a sign by the door reads "Smile, you're on camera".
blocks.frameAlt: A character walking through a convenience store towards the counter, with the wanted display at the top right
blocks.frameCredit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 11:48

blocks.title: The police are told
blocks.text: The wanted display is already showing inside the store: two gray stars and five Heat icons, among them a camera and a pistol.

blocks.title: Get out
blocks.text: They leave by the front door. The footage cuts away before a getaway is shown.
These are short clips cut together, and the door and the store may not be the same place. They show what a robbery can look like, not a set of rules.
Safes, exits
In IGN's interview Nelson robs a pawn shop without preparing, and says what he should have done.

blocks.caption: Inside a jewelry store during a robbery in the footage.
blocks.credit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 18:00

blocks.title: Prepare
blocks.text: Nelson says he should really be preparing, for example by putting a vehicle out front. He goes in without.

blocks.title: Two people, two jobs
blocks.text: IGN describes Nelson, as Jason, heading to the back to look for a safe while Lucia keeps things under control by the door.

blocks.title: Open the safe
blocks.text: He finds the safe, then tracks down its combination. He also carries an explosive, which he says would damage some of the take.

blocks.title: Leave another way
blocks.text: With police gathering at the front, he leaves by a back door.

blocks.title: The quiet way
blocks.text: In translation, Nelson describes a tool he calls a snap gun for opening a back door quietly; kicking the door in sets off the alarm. Break the security camera and you are not seen; disable the security system and the alarm stays silent, and cash can be taken from the register without anyone knowing.

blocks.title: Masks
blocks.text: If the police were told about a masked person, taking the mask off afterwards makes you harder to recognise. Nelson's advice, in translation: get out of the car and take it off.

blocks.title: Sell what you took
blocks.text: A fence who will buy shows green with a dollar sign on the map. The pair have jewelry to sell him.

blocks.title: A getaway in the footage
blocks.text: After the jewelry store, two characters leave on a motorcycle, the passenger carrying a duffel bag. The stars at that moment are hollow.
blocks.frameAlt: Two characters on a motorcycle at a junction, the passenger carrying a duffel bag
blocks.frameCredit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 18:06

blocks.text: TGG reports that loot is carried in duffel bags, with its value shown on screen, and that how many bags you can take depends on the vehicle.

items: How much each kind of target pays.
Whether a crew can be hired, and whether large robberies are planned in advance.
How long police take to arrive, and what changes it.

blocks.text: Stealing
Cars are worth money to fences, and some are harder to take and to keep than others.

blocks.title: Scan it first
blocks.text: The phone's scanner tells you whether a car is locked, alarmed or tracked, and what it is worth. In the demo it reports a car as locked, with an alarm and no tracker.
Edge, IGN and TGG give the scanner app's name as WAINK.

blocks.title: Tools
blocks.text: Nelson names a slim jim, and a key cloner for newer and luxury cars that comes later. Some parked cars cannot be taken until you have the right tool; a car with a driver in it can always be carjacked. In translation, he adds that smashing a window sets off the alarm.

blocks.title: Trackers
blocks.text: A car with what Nelson calls an advanced tracker gives its position to the police if it is driven slowly, so it has to be driven fast.

blocks.title: Taking one that is occupied
blocks.text: You can aim your weapon and tell people to get out of their car, without having to pull anybody out.
The footage shows it: a masked character aims a pistol at the driver of a car, and a second character then goes to the driver's door.

blocks.caption: A masked character aims a pistol at an occupied car.
blocks.credit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 11:37

blocks.title: Deliver it in good condition
blocks.text: A car fence pays less for a damaged car. Nelson says he can repair the car first.

blocks.title: Keep it
blocks.text: The scanner also shows what it would cost to register a car as your own.

blocks.title: Your own car
blocks.text: Your personal vehicle can be called to you, and spare outfits can be kept in its trunk.

items: How each tool is used: no source read describes a lock-picking step.
Which cars fences want, and what they pay.

blocks.text: Guns
Killing is one option among several, and what you carry is on show.

blocks.caption: A shootout in a dark office, with both bars on screen at the top left.
blocks.credit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 25:16

blocks.title: More than one way to end it
blocks.text: Nelson says a situation can be handled by threatening, knocking someone out, shooting to incapacitate, or killing. In his demo, aiming a gun without firing made the people he had angered run.

blocks.title: The yellow X
blocks.text: A yellow X when you hit someone means they are down and will not get back up.
TGG reports three hit markers: white for a hit, yellow for incapacitated, red for a kill.

blocks.title: Long guns show
blocks.text: In translation, Nelson says long guns can no longer be hidden. One on your back draws little reaction; one in your hands makes people leave or turn hostile, and the police warn you first.

blocks.title: Where your guns are kept
blocks.text: Nelson says every weapon you have bought is always available in the back of your personal vehicle. In translation, he adds that Ammu-Nation has lockers where your guns can be collected.

blocks.title: Firing to frighten
blocks.text: In translation, Nelson describes shooting near a person, not at them, to frighten or confuse them and buy time to get away.

blocks.title: Focus
blocks.text: Nelson compares Focus to Eagle Eye. TGG relays him as saying it can slow combat down.

items: How weapons are chosen: no source read describes a weapon wheel or its replacement.
Cover, beyond the fact that it exists.
Silenced weapons, melee weapons and throwables.
Ammunition: how it is bought and how much can be carried.

blocks.text: Law

Law enforcement in Leonida is about more than outrunning the officer behind you. Rockstar describes police who keep hold of what they have learned about a suspect, so it matters what they know, not only whether they can see you.

blocks.caption: Jason on a motorcycle, a police vehicle close behind.
blocks.credit: Official Rockstar Games screenshot ("Jason Duval 11"), rockstargames.com/VI/media/screenshots

blocks.text: Losing sight of the police is not necessarily the same as losing their information.
Stars and Heat at a glance

Two things sit at the top right of the screen: up to six wanted stars, and beneath them a row of small red Heat icons. The stars are the wanted level. The icons are separate, and change while the stars stay the same.

blocks.credit: Frames from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 11:48 and 14:12

frames.alt: Two gray stars above five red icons: a camera, two heads, a coat hanger, a head and a pistol
frames.label: Camera, two heads, coat hanger, head, pistol

frames.alt: Four white stars above four red icons: two heads, a coat hanger, a head and a car
frames.label: Two heads, coat hanger, head, car

blocks.text: Rob Nelson says the icons show what the police know about you. In his demo they knew what he looked like, what he was wearing, what the pair were driving, and that they were a couple. A crime has to be seen by a witness, or set off an alarm, before it is reported at all.

blocks.caption: What the police know, and what to do about it, are from Nelson's interview. Matching each to an icon is this manual's reading of the footage, not a Rockstar statement.
rows: Change your appearance: glasses, a hat, a haircut
Put on a different outfit, bought at a store or kept in your own car's trunk
Get out and take a different vehicle

blocks.caption: These two icons are in the footage, but only guides and creators say what they mean.
rows: You were caught on a security camera
The police know which weapon was used

blocks.text: Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson calls the mechanic the heat system, and describes police dispatch as very specific about what it knows.

The creator TGG, who previewed the game, quotes Nelson as saying the team wanted police to stop forgetting you the moment you lose them and to have "a bit more persistent memory." The quote comes from TGG's video, as reported by GamesRadar+; it is not in IGN's transcript.
This chapter was written before release. Exact numbers, timers, distances and thresholds are not known, and none are given here.
The wanted

blocks.caption: Four stars lit, top right, as a character fires a rifle at a police pickup.
blocks.credit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 14:08

blocks.text: The wanted display sits at the top right of the screen and has six positions. Unlit positions show as dim placeholders, and in every frame examined the lit stars are the right-most ones. Two and four stars are lit at different times.

Playing the demo, Rob Nelson described one star as not a big deal: leave the area the police are responding to and you should generally be fine. He also said things escalate if you choose to escalate them.
When the stars are hollow, the police are responding without knowing who you are, and leaving the area is enough.
What is known, level by level

blocks.caption: Only these two levels are described by Rockstar in the sources read.
rows: Not a big deal. Leave the area the police are responding to and you should generally be fine
Hard to get away by car. He suggests getting out and going on foot through the alleys

blocks.text: In the frames examined, two stars and four stars are the only counts seen lit. No frame shows one, three, five or six stars lit.
In one moment of footage the car icon disappears as the characters leave their car, while four red stars stay lit.
What it takes to reach each star has not been published. Treat any table of "this crime equals that many stars" as a guess until it has been tested in the released game.

blocks.title: How the footage was read
items: Every picture of the wanted display in this chapter is a frame from Rockstar's own Extended Look, downloaded from Rockstar's media page.
The video was examined as still frames, a few seconds apart. Times are approximate, and anything that lasts less than a few seconds, or that only shows in motion, may have been missed.

blocks.title: About the pictures
items: The large photographs in this chapter are official Rockstar screenshots chosen for their subject. They are not evidence for the rule printed beside them.
The small pictures of the wanted stars and Heat icons are different: they are frames from Rockstar's Extended Look, and the claims labelled R★ Verified rest on them.

blocks.text: The stars
Four different looks appear in Rockstar's footage. What each is seen alongside is recorded here. Rockstar has described the meaning of only one of them.

blocks.title: Hollow stars
blocks.frameAlt: Two outlined stars at the right of six positions, with no icons beneath
blocks.text: About 18:04 to 18:11. Two outlined stars with dark centres and no Heat icons, as two masked characters get onto a motorcycle across the road from a jewellers. A few seconds earlier, inside a jewelry store, a camera icon shows on its own with no stars.
blocks.frameCredit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 18:08

blocks.text: In his own demo, Nelson said hollow white stars mean the police do not know who you are: they head for the scene without a description, and leaving the area is enough. The outlined stars in this frame appear to be the same thing.

blocks.title: Gray stars
blocks.frameAlt: Two gray stars with five red icons beneath: camera, two heads, coat hanger, head, pistol
blocks.text: About 11:48 to 11:52, and again at about 12:08; frames in between show no wanted display. Two gray stars with five Heat icons beneath them. At 11:48 the scene is the inside of a convenience store. Read at six frames a second across seven seconds, the two stars stay gray throughout: they do not flash.
blocks.frameCredit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 11:48

blocks.text: One guide author, who did not attend the preview, believes gray stars mean the police hold information about you and are actively searching. No one who attended, and no one at Rockstar, mentions gray stars in the sources read.

blocks.title: White stars
blocks.frameAlt: Four white stars with four red icons beneath: two heads, coat hanger, head, car
blocks.text: About 14:04 to 14:32, and again 15:20 to 15:40, with no display for about 50 seconds between. Four white stars with four Heat icons: first while a character fires on a police pickup, then while driving a car.
blocks.frameCredit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 14:12

blocks.text: The creator TGG, who attended Rockstar's preview, says solid white stars mean the police have a direct line of sight on you. The 14:08 frame, with a police vehicle in view, is consistent with that; Rockstar has not said so in the sources read.

blocks.title: Red stars
blocks.frameAlt: Four red stars with three red icons beneath: two heads, coat hanger, head
blocks.text: About 15:50 to 16:32. Four stars are red by about 15:50. By 15:53 the car is inside a parking garage; by 15:59 two characters are on foot beside it. The moment of the change from white is not in the frames examined.
blocks.frameCredit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 16:02

blocks.text: TGG says red stars mean you have lost the officers chasing you but are still inside the area being searched: the police know who they are looking for, but not where you are.
Two GamesRadar+ writers, each reading the footage for themselves, arrive at much the same meaning; one of them writes "presumably". Rockstar has not stated it in the sources read.

Two solid white stars also appear later, at about 18:24 to 18:44, first with three icons and then with four. After the hollow stars at about 18:12, some twelve seconds of footage show no display at all, so a change from hollow to solid is not seen.

items: Flashing white stars. One creator who attended reports them for a broken line of sight, and says the Extended Look does not show them. None were found in the frames examined.
What gray stars mean. They are in the footage, but no first-hand source explains them.
How hollow stars become solid, and what turns white stars red: neither change is on screen in the frames examined.
Whether there are other appearances.

blocks.text: How police
A response starts with somebody, or something, raising the alarm.

blocks.caption: Two masked people with guns at a counter while three others raise their hands.
blocks.credit: Official Rockstar Games screenshot ("Jason and Lucia 15"), rockstargames.com/VI/media/screenshots

blocks.title: A witness
blocks.text: Nelson has said the wanted system needs someone to witness the crime for it to be reported. In his demo, a bystander called an incident in.

blocks.title: An alarm
blocks.text: The other route he names is an alarm being set off.

blocks.title: A vehicle tracker
blocks.text: Some cars carry what Nelson calls an advanced tracker, shown by a blinking red light. It tells the police where the car is if it is not driven fast enough. A scanner on the in-game phone can tell you beforehand whether a car is locked, alarmed or tracked.

blocks.caption: Interpretation: a simplified model for explanation, not a verified description of how the game works inside.
steps: It is witnessed, or an alarm or tracker is tripped
Police try to identify and find the suspect

blocks.title: Do not read too much into this
items: Nelson was describing the open world. Missions and scripted events may behave differently.
Being noticed is not the same as being identified: see the next pages.

blocks.text: Heat:
Heat is the information the police hold about you. On screen it appears as small icons with the wanted stars.

blocks.caption: Lucia, with a patrol officer and police lights behind her.
blocks.credit: Official Rockstar Games screenshot ("Lucia Caminos 14"), rockstargames.com/VI/media/screenshots

blocks.text: Nelson points to icons on screen that show what the police know. In his demo they knew what he looked like, what he was wearing, what the pair were driving, and that they were a couple.
In the footage the icons are small red discs in a row beneath the stars. Six different ones appear: a camera, two heads, a coat hanger, a single head, a pistol and a car. Up to five show at once.

blocks.caption: Five Heat icons beneath two gray stars: camera, two heads, coat hanger, head and pistol.
blocks.credit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 11:48

blocks.text: One guide says the more icons are active, the harder the police are to lose.

blocks.title: Appearance
blocks.text: The police know what you look like. Glasses, a hat or a new haircut change your appearance, but not what you are wearing.

blocks.title: Clothing
blocks.text: The police know your outfit. Nelson calls an outfit they have seen compromised.

blocks.title: Vehicle
blocks.text: The police know what you are driving.
Evidence that can

blocks.title: Accomplice
blocks.text: The police can know that Jason and Lucia are together.

blocks.title: Weapon
blocks.text: A pistol icon appears among the Heat icons at about 11:48.
Guides read the pistol icon as the police knowing which weapon was used. Rockstar has not described it in the sources read.

blocks.title: Security camera
blocks.frameAlt: A single red camera icon above the ammunition counter, with no stars
blocks.frameCredit: Frame from "Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look", Rockstar Games, about 18:02
blocks.text: A camera icon appears on its own, with no stars, inside a jewelry store at about 18:01 to 18:03; it is gone when the stars appear a second later. It also appears among five icons at 11:48.
Guides and creators read the camera icon as being caught on security camera. Rockstar has not described it in the sources read.
Several icons can be active at once, and the set changes while the stars are showing. Whether there are more than these six is not known.
Heat can rise as well as fall: in the demo, putting a bystander out of action raised it.

blocks.title: About the icons
items: The icon pictures in this chapter are frames from Rockstar's official footage, not redrawn artwork.
What each icon is called, and exactly what it does, will be rechecked after launch.

blocks.text: Wanted state
Being chased and being known are two different things. This is the idea the rest of the chapter depends on.

blocks.caption: Two officers beside a Vice Beach Police car at night.
blocks.credit: Official Rockstar Games screenshot ("Vice City 06"), rockstargames.com/VI/media/screenshots

What identifying information police have kept
Whether officers can currently see you
Where police keep looking after the incident

blocks.caption: Interpretation: a conceptual guide based on published pre-release descriptions, not a verified internal state diagram.

blocks.text: Nelson uses "heat" in two ways: for what the police know about you, and for the police searching an area ("we have heat now"). This manual keeps the two apart, but the game may not.
The two can come apart. At one point in the demo Nelson notes that the pair have got away with no heat; shortly after, police searching the area means they have heat again.
GamesRadar+, reporting the creator TGG's preview, says clues can still get you recognised later, even after the wanted stars have gone.
Finding
You are expected to look for the police, not read them off the map.

blocks.caption: Jason behind a chain-link fence with a pistol raised, as an armed figure approaches under police lights.
blocks.credit: Official Rockstar Games screenshot ("Jason Duval 07"), rockstargames.com/VI/media/screenshots

blocks.text: Nelson describes Focus as much like Eagle Eye in Red Dead Redemption 2: a way to locate things you want to find, and certainly police. In IGN's account of the demo it made a nearby officer glow.

TGG also quotes Nelson as saying that police do not show up on the radar and do show up when you use Focus, and that this is harder but more fun, depending on the wanted level. Again this is TGG's account, reported by GamesRadar+.
That Focus shows police through walls is TGG's own description, not a Nelson quote.
One guide, reading the footage, suggests that at higher wanted levels the minimap is washed out by red and blue flashing light.

blocks.text: Hot
Getting away from the scene may not make the scene safe to come back to.

blocks.caption: Patrol cars gathered on a bridge, a boat with flashing lights below and a helicopter sweeping a searchlight overhead.
blocks.credit: Official Rockstar Games screenshot ("Vice City 17"), rockstargames.com/VI/media/screenshots

blocks.text: Checking the map in his demo, Nelson calls the place of an incident a hot area: the police are there and will hang around for a while, and the map still shows a star over it.

VICE, relaying creators' previews, calls it the active search area and says red stars mean you have escaped the chase but are still inside it. One guide describes a red zone with a lighter ring around it. What the game itself calls the area on screen is not confirmed.

blocks.title: Leave
blocks.text: At a low wanted level, getting out of the area the police are responding to is described as enough.

blocks.title: Wait
blocks.text: With police searching an area, one option Nelson lists is to wait for it to die down.

blocks.title: Coming back too soon
blocks.text: Nelson says that if you go back, the police will still be hanging around for a while.
One creator says he was told that at the highest wanted level the search covers the whole map. Treat this as hearsay until tested.

items: The size of a hot area, how long it lasts and how it shrinks.
How each wanted level changes it.
Whether a change of outfit clears heat while you are still inside a hot area: published accounts differ.

Each clue has its own answer. Most of these come from Rob Nelson's own demo; none is a guaranteed escape.

blocks.text: With three stars in the city, Nelson says getting away by car can be hard unless it is very fast, and that the best option is usually to get off the streets and go on foot through the alleys.

In the Extended Look the car icon is present at about 15:56, when the car has stopped in a garage bay with its door open, and is gone three seconds later, when the character is on foot beside it. The stars are red throughout. This is one moment of footage, not a stated rule.

blocks.text: One guide states that splitting up does not let you sacrifice your partner: if either is caught, you are busted.
Nelson's advice throughout: don't draw attention to yourself, and you should be fine.
Police
What has been described about police tactics and equipment so far. This page will grow after release.

blocks.caption: A patrol car alongside a dirt bike, with a police helicopter overhead.
blocks.credit: Official Rockstar Games screenshot ("Jason and Lucia 09"), rockstargames.com/VI/media/screenshots

blocks.title: They go to the scene
blocks.text: Without a description, police head for where the crime happened. In the demo's store robbery, Nelson expects officers to gather out front, and leaves by a back door.

blocks.title: You can stand and fight
blocks.text: Nelson says you can stay and fight the police if you want to.

blocks.title: Chases in missions
blocks.text: Where a mission turns into a chase or a robbery, Rockstar says it tries to keep it consistent with how those systems work in the open world. Your partner can drive while you deal with pursuers.

blocks.title: Patrol car equipment
blocks.text: One creator believes police cars carry shotguns or rifles in the trunk, sometimes body armor, and a tracker. VICE relays this; it is not confirmed.

blocks.title: Cars, a boat and a helicopter
blocks.text: One official screenshot shows patrol cars on a bridge, a boat with flashing police lights on the water below and a helicopter sweeping a searchlight. What brings each of them, and at which wanted level, is not known.
